questions.stem: Bernard, 67, is in ED with decompensated heart failure. He says he takes all his prescribed tablets every day. He has no chest pain, palpitations, fever or sputum. He mentions that his big toe was 'agony' a couple of weeks ago but has now settled. Which question is most likely to uncover the trigger for his decompensation?
options: "Has your GP changed the dose of any of your heart tablets lately?"
"Did you take anything for the toe, such as tablets bought from the chemist?"
"Have you been eating more salty food or takeaway meals recently?"
"Have you been drinking more fluid than usual over the last week?"
questions.why: A recent gout flare in someone with heart failure should make you ask straight away about over-the-counter NSAIDs. Ibuprofen causes sodium and water retention, and taken with a diuretic and an ARB it also causes AKI (the 'triple whammy'). Patients often don't count chemist medicines as 'tablets', so ask about them directly.
notes: A recent dose change is worth asking about, but the gout history points to an unreported over-the-counter medicine as the more likely trigger here.
Too much salt is a common trigger, but nothing in the history points to it, while the painful toe points to self-treatment with an NSAID.
Too much fluid can cause decompensation, but the gout flare is the clue in this case, and it points to an NSAID rather than fluid intake.

questions.stem: Bernard, 67, is being admitted from ED with acute decompensated heart failure. RR 26, SpO2 91% on room air, BP 144/86, warm peripheries. Creatinine is 132 µmol/L (baseline 86). His usual diuretic is furosemide 40 mg orally each morning. Which initial diuretic order is most appropriate?
options: Furosemide 20 mg IV now, using a lower dose because of the AKI
Furosemide 40 to 80 mg IV now, repeated according to response
Furosemide 80 mg orally now, double his usual morning dose
Furosemide 250 mg IV infusion over 1 hour now, then review
questions.why: In acute decompensation the IV loop diuretic dose should be at least his usual oral daily dose, up to about 2.5 times it (so 40 to 80 mg IV here). Then titrate to urine output, daily weights and daily UEC.
notes: The congestion is driving the AKI, so it is not a reason to cut the dose. A dose below his usual one is unlikely to relieve the congestion.
When the gut wall is oedematous, oral furosemide is poorly absorbed. A patient who is hypoxic and breathless at rest needs IV treatment.
This is a high dose meant for diuretic resistance. It is excessive as a first dose and raises the risk of ototoxicity and electrolyte upset.

questions.stem: Bernard, 67, takes furosemide and candesartan for heart failure. He took ibuprofen for 5 days for gout and his creatinine is now 132 µmol/L (baseline 86). Which mechanism best explains how the ibuprofen reduced his glomerular filtration rate?
options: It blocked prostaglandin-mediated dilatation of the afferent arteriole
It blocked angiotensin II-mediated constriction of the efferent arteriole
It caused direct toxic injury to proximal tubular cells, giving ATN
It inhibited the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
questions.why: When kidney perfusion falls, prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, which together keep glomerular pressure up. NSAIDs remove the afferent dilatation and the ARB removes the efferent constriction. Add volume loss from the diuretic and the GFR falls.
notes: This is how candesartan (the ARB) contributes to the triple whammy, not how ibuprofen does.
NSAID kidney injury here is caused by changes in blood flow, not direct tubular toxicity; aminoglycosides and contrast are classic direct tubular toxins.
This is how furosemide works; ibuprofen does not act on NKCC2.

questions.stem: You examine Bernard, 67, to assess his jugular venous pressure. He is sitting at 45° with his head turned slightly to the left. Where should you look for the pulsation of the right internal jugular vein?
options: Superficial to sternocleidomastoid, crossing the muscle obliquely downwards
In the suprasternal notch, medial to the sternal head of sternocleidomastoid
In the posterior triangle, lateral to the clavicular head of sternocleidomastoid
Deep to sternocleidomastoid, between its two heads, rising towards the earlobe
questions.why: The internal jugular vein runs deep to sternocleidomastoid. Low in the neck it lies between the sternal and clavicular heads, and it runs up towards the earlobe. It drains in a straight line, without valves, through the brachiocephalic vein and SVC into the right atrium. Measure the JVP as the vertical height above the sternal angle.
notes: This is the course of the external jugular vein, which can be kinked or affected by valves and is less reliable for estimating right atrial pressure.
The internal jugular vein lies lateral to the trachea and the sternal head, not in the suprasternal notch.
The posterior triangle lies outside the line of the internal jugular vein; pulsation there is more likely the external jugular vein or the subclavian artery.
